analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products, restrict their marketing, and require ingredient disclosure.
analysis.headline: The tobacco-regulation bill was introduced with 5 sponsors and 2 additional cosponsors, referred to the Senate Health Committee, and never received a vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The KIDS Act would have put tobacco products under the same federal health law that governs drugs and medical devices, giving the Secretary of Health and Human Services power to set manufacturing standards, restrict marketing and advertising, review mail-order sales to minors, require ingredient disclosure, and stop companies from claiming a product is safer without proof. The bill was introduced by Senator Tom Harkin in February 2001 with several cosponsors and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat without action for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers who would face tighter restrictions on tobacco marketing, advertising, and access, including review of mail-order sales to minors. Smokers and their families would benefit from ingredient disclosure, manufacturing standards, recall authority, and a scientific review of at what nicotine levels products become addictive. The public would gain the right to know what is in cigarette brands.

how_it_helps.text: The bill authorizes the Secretary of Health and Human Services to regulate any tobacco product as a drug or device under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, subjecting it to federal health regulation for the first time at this scale.
It directs the Secretary to review and restrict mail-order sales to people under 18 and to impose additional restrictions on marketing, advertising, and youth access.

It requires manufacturers to disclose all ingredients and nicotine content for each brand, submit safety assessments for new ingredients, and submit to FDA inspection of factories, records, and internal research on addiction and marketing.
It prohibits companies from making reduced-risk or 'safer' health claims unless the Secretary finds, based on scientific evidence, that the product significantly reduces overall health risk.

It requires a scientific advisory committee to evaluate whether a level of nicotine exists at which products do not cause dependence, and gives the Secretary authority to set product performance standards, including reducing or eliminating nicotine.
It preserves state and local governments' ability to impose stricter tobacco controls, and gives the Secretary recall authority over dangerous tobacco products.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would bear the cost of ingredient disclosure, safety assessments, good-manufacturing-practice compliance, factory inspections, marketing restrictions, and bans on unsubstantiated 'reduced risk' claims. Tobacco leaf growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives are explicitly exempt from the bill. Some compliance costs could be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly exempts tobacco leaf growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives from its requirements, leaving the farming side of the industry outside federal oversight.

Its warning-label preemption clause bars states from requiring any additional warning labels beyond the federal ones, which some public-health advocates have historically opposed as a ceiling on state action — though the bill preserves most other state and local tobacco authority.

Funding depends on an annual appropriation and includes a trigger: no expenditures are allowed in any year when FDA funding is lower than the prior year, so the regulatory program could be stalled by the appropriations process.
Compliance costs for manufacturers — ingredient testing, safety assessments, and manufacturing upgrades — could be passed on to consumers in cigarette prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefits are large and well established: tobacco is the leading cause of preventable death in the United States, and the bill's main tools — youth access and marketing restrictions, ingredient disclosure, manufacturing standards, and control over health claims — target how companies recruit and keep customers. The main structural weaknesses are the carve-out for tobacco growers and a funding mechanism vulnerable to appropriation fights. The compliance burden falls on a small number of large manufacturers whose business model depends on addictive products; any price increase to consumers is the cost of a regulation aimed at reducing consumption itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health Committee in February 2001, and the committee never took it up before the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the KIDS Act on February 6, 2001, joined by Senators Chafee, Graham, Bingaman, and Johnson as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day it was introduced.
No further action was recorded: the committee never marked up the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor for a vote during the 107th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers were better off because the bill never advanced: they avoided federal ingredient disclosure, factory inspections, marketing restrictions, and the ban on unproven reduced-risk claims. No comparable federal regime covered these areas at the time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco manufacturers, unregulated by the FDA

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the KIDS Act to give the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to regulate tobacco products, restrict youth marketing, and require ingredient disclosure.

for.name: Sens. Chafee, Graham, Bingaman, and Johnson
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 6, 2001 and never scheduled a markup or advanced it to the floor for the remainder of the 107th Congress.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The bill's provisions — marketing restrictions, ingredient disclosure, manufacturing standards, and control of health claims — would have imposed major costs on them; the record does not document their involvement in this bill's fate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — 6 of 49 Democratic and 1 of 49 Republican senators as cosponsors alongside the Democratic sponsor — but no vote was ever held, so the parties' positions were never tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected cigarette and smokeless tobacco makers to FDA regulation, ingredient and research disclosure, factory inspections, marketing restrictions, and a ban on unproven 'reduced risk' claims. Their interest in blocking it ran against the public-health purpose of the bill.

Retailers and distributors would have had to verify compliance with access, advertising, and labeling rules, including advertising restrictions for outlets accessible to minors. Mail-order sellers faced possible restriction or elimination of sales to minors.

industries.industry: Tobacco growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts tobacco leaf producers from its scope and bars the Secretary from regulating tobacco farming or entering farms without consent, leaving growers outside federal oversight.
